mcqs.question: What is the main difference between a cold start and a warm start?
options: A cold start must provision and initialize a fresh execution environment before running the handler; a warm start reuses an already-initialized one
A cold start runs on cheaper hardware than a warm start
A warm start skips executing the handler entirely
A cold start only happens for HTTP-triggered functions
mcqs.explanation: The setup work — sandbox allocation, runtime init, dependency loading — is what a cold start pays for and a warm start skips by reusing a live environment. Hardware cost and trigger type aren't what distinguishes the two.

mcqs.question: Provisioned concurrency shrinks cold starts by:
options: Automatically reducing the size of the function's deployment package
Keeping a set number of execution environments pre-initialized and warm at all times, at the cost of a standing charge
Increasing the platform's concurrency limit for the function
Switching the function to a faster programming language automatically
mcqs.explanation: Provisioned concurrency pre-pays to keep environments ready, trading away pure pay-per-use savings for predictable low latency — it doesn't touch package size, concurrency limits, or language choice.

mcqs.question: A function's concurrency limit is reached during a traffic burst. What happens to additional invocations?
options: They run instantly, sharing the same environment as an existing invocation
The platform automatically raises the limit with no configuration needed
They queue or get throttled until an execution environment becomes available
They are billed at zero cost since they didn't run
mcqs.explanation: Concurrency limits are hard caps — invocations beyond the limit wait or are rejected, they don't silently share an environment or auto-raise the ceiling.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't a multi-hour video transcoding job fit the FaaS execution model well?
options: FaaS platforms cannot process video file formats
Video processing requires a GPU, which no FaaS platform ever provides
FaaS functions cannot be triggered by file uploads
Every platform enforces a maximum execution time per invocation, far shorter than a multi-hour job needs
mcqs.explanation: The hard execution-time cap, not file format or trigger type, is what rules out long-running work — it has to be re-architected as shorter steps or moved to a container/VM.
